Anyway, console manufacturers really need to grasp the importance of backwards compatibility.

Yes, it may be costly to implement, or technologically tricky, if you went off the rails and created a really bizarre architecture in your previous generation that you have now abandoned in your current release, but you will never storm and corner the market, until you do.

Mainly because there will always be a sizeable percentage of that market who are still tied to the previous generation. They sunk a lot of money into their libraries, and will be reluctant to invest in a new console that will render their current library useless, save to be used as crappy tea coasters, or in amateur art projects.

That's a really good point. I'm still impressed that Microsoft kind of pulled a bait and switch on Sony this gen. Neither console maker was too worried about backwards compatibility at launch because their competition didn't have it either. But Microsoft surprised everyone with the announcement over a year later and caught Sony with nothing in the works. It's definitely a good selling point for the Xbox right now.

Sony screwed themselves over big time with Playstation Now. They could implement Backwards Compatibility. It might be technologically challenging, but it is not beyond their means.

However, to do so would take away a large part of the incentive to pay for Playstation Now, as that is currently the only way to play a previous gen game on a PS4.

I think backwards compatibility will be easier in the future. X86_64 has been around for over 40 years at this point and nothing else seems to be in a position to overtake it. I am willing to bet the PS5 and "Next Box" (has anyone figured out Microsoft's naming scheme yet?) will also be x86_64 based. The reason why the 360 was because PowerPC used to be much more efficient than x86_64, and made a lot of sense for non-general purpose computing. the PS3 was a lot closer to the old days of consoles, when each system had a dramatically different architecture and the developers were expected to write a good portion of their software in assembly tailored to that console.

I was fully expecting for there to be no backwards compatibility at all this generation because of the major architectural differences. I think Microsoft has surprised everyone with their support.

It's also worth mentioning that what Microsoft has done is incredible. No one thought that they would be able to get remotely close to acceptable performance. This is why Sony focused on streaming content. They figured they would get better performance from that than from making a compatibility layer.

TLDR:

Backwards compatibility will be a non-issue for the next generation because it will be trivial to implement as long as x86_64 remains the dominant processor architecture.
